identity.real_world_identity_notes: The submitted R89C maps to Nissan's 1989 Lola/Nissan Group C sports prototype. Nissan Heritage identifies the R89C and specifies a five-speed VGC transmission; Motorsport Magazine independently identifies the Hewland VGC five-speed and reverse transaxle. An exact-model community specification describes the selector as a dogleg H-shifter, but the reviewed authoritative sources do not establish the VGC's internal synchronizer/dog construction or the driver's running clutch/blip technique. Real wheel topology remains unknown.

wheel_rim.notes: Exact real-car wheel details were not established by the reviewed sources.

A separate exact-model technical reference supplies the dogleg H-shifter description as lower-confidence selector evidence. No existing curated record matches.

claims.basis: Nissan's official Heritage Collection identifies the 1989 R89C and its VGC five-speed transmission. Motorsport Magazine corroborates the exact Lola/Nissan Group C identity and VGC gearbox. A separate exact-model technical reference supplies the dogleg H-shifter description as lower-confidence selector evidence. No existing curated record matches.

Nissan specifies VGC five-speed and Motor Sport Magazine specifies five-speed plus reverse. The exact-model technical reference describes a dogleg H-shifter, and the period cockpit account describes the driver selecting numbered gears. Confidence is medium because the selector wording comes from a community reference. The R89C is documented with a manual five-speed VGC and an H-pattern selector; a driver-operated H-pattern manual requires clutch control to pull away from rest. The claim is mechanism-based, not simulator-derived. No upshift blip action is described; the unresolved mechanism does not justify inventing one. No upshift automatic blip action is described. The reviewed sources do not prescribe a separate downshift throttle-lift step. No downshift automatic cut procedure is described for the manually selected VGC transmission.
